conservation.notes: Protected in the United States under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act of 1918.

human_tolerance.notes: Holds territory over tall grass, cattails and other thick upright vegetation, which is why it colonises the edges of ditches, hedgerows, wet lawns and unmown field margins close to houses.

phases.name: territorial
phases.note: Males return to last year's territory and sing from tall vegetation; territorial activity starts earlier when a winter has left a lot of standing residual vegetation.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: Polygynous: one male holds a territory containing several nesting females. Most females in Ohio breed in upland hay and legume fields rather than in scarce wetland.

phases.name: moult
phases.note: The critical period of the complete post-breeding moult runs from late August into October, when the missing remiges and rectrices slow the bird down; almost all birds have finished by mid-October.

phases.name: flocking
phases.note: Birds gather in enormous loose flocks on winter fields, feedlots and roosts.

vocalizations.description: The male's territorial song, a liquid gurgling 'conk-la-reee' delivered from the top of a reed, cattail or tall grass, often for a long time from one perch. He also gives a shorter 'conk' call in flight and a hoarse 'chaarr' when chased from a perch by another male.
A sharp metallic 'chack' or 'chick' given by either sex when flushed or when a predator comes near the nest; the female also uses it to scold intruders at the nest.

external.note: GBIF usageKey 9409198 and family Icteridae from the GBIF Backbone record for the accepted name; iNaturalist taxon id 9744 from the iNaturalist taxa API; ITIS TSN 179045 from the ITISWebService scientific-name search, which returns Agelaius phoeniceus (Linnaeus, 1766) as an exact match; Wikidata Q754043 from a Wikidata entity search for the scientific name.

conservation.note: IUCN category from Wikidata P141, which points at the IUCN 'Least Concern' item; the species is one of the most abundant birds in North America, so the article carries no threat narrative.

range.note: Country list derived from the article's 'breeds from Alaska and Newfoundland south to Florida, the Gulf of Mexico, Mexico, and Guatemala, with isolated populations in western El Salvador, northwestern Honduras, and northwestern Costa Rica'.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: The bird walks on the ground to forage in grass and short field crops, and powers its flight, gliding between foraging bouts; the three modes are authored from that behaviour.

traits.nest_type.note: The article describes nesting in the dense bases of upright vegetation in marshes and fields, which is an open cup nest; the schema has no marsh-nest category, so Cup is the closest and the site is carried in habitat.resources as nest_cup.

traits.mass_kg.note: Midpoint of the male range 'weighing between 65 and 80 g'. The male is the strongly marked bird the record draws, and males are the ones that hold and defend the display perches.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: 'males weighing between 65 and 80 g ... the females about 35 g'.

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of the male's 'between 22 and 24 cm'; the female's '17 or 18 cm' is recorded in the range note rather than the headline length, because the male is the plumage drawn.

traits.lifespan_y.note: The article ranks the red-winged blackbird among the best-studied wild birds in the world and records an individually known bird that was still breeding at eight years old; 12 is an authored middle estimate, not a figure the article states.

traits.diet.note: 'Seeds and insects make up the bulk of the red-winged blackbird's diet', with foraging on old grasses, alfalfa and legume hay and on the insects these hold. The 0.55/0.45 split is a judgement that keeps both roughly equal, leaning seed because the winter flocks feed on fields and feedlots.

traits.social.note: Polygynous: one territorial male holds a territory with several nesting females, and outside the breeding season birds gather in very large flocks. The upper group size is a judgement scaled well below the huge flocks the article describes, because the scene is one garden.

traits.defense.note: 'The red shoulder patches ... are vital in the defense of the territory': when the red patches were dyed black, 64% of males lost their territories against 8% of controls, and males chase off non-territorial rivals. That is a display-and-chase defence by the male, which is Mob rather than Flee.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement at 0.45: it lives in open fields and farm crops right up to farm buildings and settles readily on mown and unmown grass near houses, but it needs tall vegetation to feel safe and will leave a small, tidy plot.

habitat.use.note: 'It generally prefers wetlands and inhabits both freshwater and saltwater marshes, particularly if cattail is present. It is also found in dry upland areas, where it inhabits meadows, prairies, and old fields', plus 'sparse deciduous forests'; the ground/arboreal/aquatic split is authored from those four habitat statements.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Roosts in tall dense vegetation, especially cattail and reed beds, and in the shrub and hedge layer of a field edge.

habitat.resources.note: The seed-and-insect diet sentence, split by season because the winter flocks feed in fields on seed while the breeding-season diet is the insects taken from tall grass and hay, plus the perch, shelter and nest-site sentences. The article's Ohio work gives the months: territorial males are on station from late February, and nesting runs through early summer.

habitat.requires.note: The habitat paragraphs are emphatic that the bird is 'attracted to tall vegetation that restricts visibility' and prefers thick-stemmed plants and old upright residual growth, so a territorial bird is only ever modelled within 30 m of a song perch. 30 m is an authored radius: the article gives no distance.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: It occupies agricultural land, alfalfa and hay fields and field edges, so it lives beside farms and suburbs; the numeric tolerances are authored, and `uses_gardens` follows from the same field-edge behaviour with the tall-grass requirement as the limit.

seasonal.strategy.note: 'Northern populations are generally migratory, moving south to Mexico and the Southern United States', but it 'may winter as far north as Pennsylvania and British Columbia', so Ohio birds are resident for much of the year and only northern populations clear out: PartialMigration.

seasonal.winter_fraction.note: Judgement at 0.7: northern and western populations leave for Mexico and the southern United States while the south-central and Great Lakes populations, which are most of an Ohio winter flock, stay.

seasonal.phases.note: The territorial, breeding, moult and flocking phases all come from the article: males defend territories from tall vegetation; the Wood County, Ohio study of 1964-1968 puts the breeding bird in that county in alfalfa and legume hay; the critical moult period is 'from late August to early September' with almost all birds finished by mid-October; and the winter behaviour is enormous flocks. The day-level boundaries are judgements.

seasonal.life_stages.note: 'It acquires its adult plumage only after the breeding season of the year following its birth when it is between thirteen and fifteen months of age', and the first pre-basic molt 'generally begins 45-60 days after individuals have left the nest'; duration_days 45 and scale 0.9 are judgements for the streaked brown juvenile.

vocalizations.song.note: The male's territorial song and the display-perch behaviour are long established in the article and the wider literature; the description is limited to what the article records and no openly licensed recording is cited for this species, so no `recordings` entry is claimed.

vocalizations.alarm.note: Authored from the general account of the male-male chase and the flush of a foraging bird; the loudness and cooldown are the field's own judgement, and no recording is cited.

look.note: 'the male is all black with a red shoulder and yellow wing bar, while the female is a nondescript dark brown', with black eyes, bill and feet and a sharply pointed bill. The red-and-yellow epaulets are drawn as extra parts on the wings because the article treats the shoulder patch as the bird's signature. The proportions are authored from the 22-24 cm length and 31-40 cm wingspan.

behavior.note: bt-perching-songbird-v1 is the shared program for a bird that holds a defended territory, sings from a song perch, roosts in cover, builds a nest and takes food on the ground; flee_m is set above the 6 m default because this bird is bolder and defends a territory rather than withdrawing, and food_tag is seed because the winter flock diet is field seed.
